🚀 I’ve been featured in Startups Magazine!

I’m excited to share my thoughts on how increasingly accessible AI could give SMEs a competitive advantage when competing with larger businesses.

For many smaller businesses, growth has traditionally meant making a big investment upfront: hiring more people, building specialist teams and taking on extra operational costs before the revenue is guaranteed.

AI is starting to change that equation.

It can help SMEs:
→ Give their existing teams the capacity to take on more work
→ Access research and analytical capabilities that were previously difficult to afford
→ Pursue bigger contracts and test new products or services with less operational pressure
→ Free up people to focus on relationships, specialist expertise and higher-value work

The real opportunity is to turn those capabilities into commercial outcomes: winning new business, entering new markets and growing without costs increasing at the same rate.

As an SME founder myself, I find this shift incredibly exciting. Smaller businesses have an opportunity to think more ambitiously about what they can achieve.

Thank you to the Startups Magazine team for featuring my article!

After a little break, I'm continuing to chronicle each of my five years freelancing with more transparency than I've shown before. This is YEAR THREE. The bad year. Links to the others in the comments.

Year Three is the year ChatGPT comes out. I lose three clients almost overnight. I sympathise with the creative agencies; they're losing work too. The others say it's nothing to do with AI. Sure. I have bits here and there, but it’s not enough to sustain me. 

I begrudgingly get certified with a number of AI tools and spend a hideous amount of time applying to jobs. After a few months of bleakness, I am ready to leave freelancing. I open up my search to part-time and full-time. 

Within months of this revolutionary technology hitting the market, I am asked to summarise what the rise in generative AI means for content and SEO in a 30-second, one-way interview. They create a brand detractor for life. Still, it's an insight into the pressures on writers and marketers to have it figured out with little data. 

After six months, I get a full-time offer I’m really excited about. I provisionally accept, but they're hit by a hiring freeze the day I’m supposed to receive my contract.

I do some extra-ing on movie sets, something I've always enjoyed but that is not stable. I look after friends’ dogs to get out of the house. I exercise a lot, but then break my ankle. My mental health takes a nose dive. I only realise later that in the fog, I did not ask a single person for help. 

I write articles in a few magazines, and the pay is often shockingly low. I get offered a couple of gigs to train AI models to write better. I’m desperate, but I reject them. I explain that while I’m not naive enough to think AI won’t change everything, I'm also not going to build systems that help kill a craft I love. I also turn down offers to edit hundreds of thousands of AI-generated words for under minimum wage.

I direct most of my energy to AI upskilling and build a website called Stubborn Travel. I run SEO experiments on content that is human vs. AI-generated vs. AI-assisted. I’m depressed that this seems to be my new path, but feel I need to future-proof myself.

At the end of the year, the tides begin to turn. People start to notice that while AI can generate a lot of content, people don't like that content. I pick up two huge clients, both through freelance marketplaces. While my skills kept them as clients, I believe landing them was total luck. Luck for being in the right place at the right time, and luck in a way, for having so few bookings that I could start immediately as they both required.

I work a crazy amount the final months. I'm overbooked, working evenings, weekends, everything. Turning down clients. I'm stressed but so grateful. Thanks to these months, my income Year 3 was the same as Year 1 and 2, or around 20% less than my former full-time job. If you just looked at the numbers, you'd think I'd had three years of smooth sailing.

Year 4 and 5 coming soon.

The In-House Legal Salary Guide 2027 for the North of England and the Regions is finished. 📊

It covers salaries, bonuses, benefits, interim day rates, notice periods and what is actually moving the market. And it is built from the roles we recruit for and the offers we negotiate, not guesswork.

A few things that jumped out while putting it together:

🔸 There is a real squeeze between £60k and £100k. Plenty of highly capable lawyers sit at Senior Legal Counsel level for 10 to 12 years PQE and struggle to get beyond £100k, even with supervisory responsibility. For many, the move to another organisation is the most effective route to a promotion or a meaningful pay rise.

🔸 Hybrid is now the baseline. 70% of in-house roles are hybrid, with four day weeks and defined core hours increasingly part of the negotiation.

🔸 At levels below Head of Legal, moving sector can deliver a bigger salary jump than a change in job title alone.

🔸 Employment, data and regulatory lawyers remain in short supply, as do commercial lawyers with technology and AI contract expertise.

I am not putting the full guide on LinkedIn, so if you would like a copy, send me an email or a message and I will get it over to you. Whether you are a lawyer curious about where you sit or a hiring manager benchmarking your team, it should be useful.

A job posting reads differently once you check the contract type, and this one matters.
United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) lists the Artificial Intelligence (AI) Innovation Analyst position or role at International Personnel Services Agreement-9 (IPSA-9), based in Bonn, open to internal and external applicants, with a deadline of 24th November 2026. The one(1)-day difference reflects time zones, and United Nations Development Programme's (UNDP’s) own date is the safer one to plan around. Because the contract is a personnel agreement and not a staff appointment, benefits and entitlements differ, so read the vacancy terms before assuming “United Nations (UN) salary and benefits.”

The UK now has a sovereign AI venture fund. The part I think many founders are missing is what sits alongside the investment.

Sovereign AI’s offer beyond investment has three live routes.

The R&D Procurement Scheme is the big one. It has up to £100m until March 2030 for UK startups and SMEs to build new AI against challenges set by government. Contracts run from £250k to £10m, with most expected to be £1m to £3m. It’s a contract rather than a grant, so government becomes your first customer, and you keep your IP.

There are four challenges at the moment:

- AI for a more productive NHS
- integrating AI across defence mission environments, particularly at the edge
- compute efficiency for public AI infrastructure
- safe adoption of AI agents, run with the NCSC

There’s no minimum turnover or trading history. Small companies that are short on cash can ask for upfront payments.

The bar is high, though. You need at least 4 out of 5 on every assessment criterion to progress. The work has to be genuine R&D, roughly TRL 4 to 8, and you have to do at least half of it yourself.

Timing matters - you first apply to join the approved supplier list, which takes up to two weeks, and you should do that at least two weeks before the deadline you’re aiming for. Batch 2 opens on 14 November and closes on 31 December. Batch 3 closes on 26 February.

There are two other routes:

1. Compute through the AI Research Resource: up to a million GPU hours for strategically significant AI R&D.
2. Visa reimbursement: for companies already receiving Sovereign AI support that are hiring international R&D talent.

There’s also a Strategic Assets grant programme, for building shared AI datasets and autonomous lab infrastructure. Its first £9m round closed in June. A larger programme of up to £160m is expected to follow, subject to approvals, so it’s one to watch if you’re sitting on valuable data or lab capability. 

For most early AI companies, the first paying customer is the hardest thing to land. A route where government is that customer is worth a serious look.

Dear managers who like to reduce HR to “the girl who does the paperwork” ...
HIRING NO LONGER LOOKS LIKE A FUNNEL.
It looks like a dumbbell.

Johnny Campbell broke down the entire hiring process, from the decision to open a role to the signed contract, into 80 steps. 80!
Eighty. Then he asked how many of them actually have to be done by a human.
Eighteen. 18!

More interesting than the number is where those eighteen sit.
Almost all of them at the very beginning and the very end.

At the beginning, someone experienced has to decide whether to open the role at all, who we are realistically looking for, and which requirements really matter and which are just decoration in the job ad.
AI doesn’t know this.
It needs context about the company, the market and the people, and the recruiter or hiring manager has to supply it.

Only then can AI take the middle: search, first contact, sorting profiles, screening, scheduling.

There it is faster than any of us, and it never gets bored.

And at the end, the human comes back. Is this really the right candidate? Does reality match what we found out? Do we want to work with this person?
No software will take responsibility for that decision.

That’s why it’s not a funnel. It’s a dumbbell: heavy at both ends, thin in the middle.

The future of hiring isn’t recruiter versus AI. Without a recruiter, AI just processes a badly defined task faster.
Without AI, the recruiter spends most of their time on work that doesn’t need their experience at all.

So AI doesn’t reduce the value of recruiters.
It increases it. The winner won’t be the company that buys the most AI.
It will be the one that puts it in the hands of people who know who they are looking for.
HR is only getting more important. Dear managers who like to reduce HR to “the girl who does the paperwork”. :)

OpenAI and Upwork just published a 24-page study on how AI is reshaping freelance work (link in 1st comment).

You might be tempted to focus on the drop in content writing job posts, which fell ~31% YoY on Upwork while making up 14.5% of sampled ChatGPT conversations.

But the more interesting tidbit is further down in the report. For comparable work in the same month and subcategory: 

> Fixed-price project budgets for AI-related jobs are 52.4% higher. 
> Hours logged in the first 90 days on hourly contracts are 40.6% higher. 
> Posted hourly rates are only 1.5% higher.

So clients aren't paying an hourly premium just because someone puts AI in their bio, but they're looking to buy larger, rebundled scopes of work that can demonstrate superior value through proper AI use. 

We can also see that 98.6% of the 'uncommon task pairs' showing up in AI job posts are familiar tasks that used to be done by separate people, so instead of hiring one freelancer to write copy/1500 words on Z topic, another to edit visuals, and a third to wire up marketing automation, teams are looking hire one operator who can connect the whole workflow, end-to-end.

So businesses on Upwork still pay for human judgment & end-to-end delivery: turning raw customer research into a finished page, a working template, or a connected campaign without three layers of handoffs... or two-three people doing specialist work.

My own anecdotal experience over the past three years also confirms this. I've been doing both SEO and content together rather than treating them as separate functions with a handoff -- having also managed bigger teams, I've seen both sides. I don't know how to feel about it just yet because a) the cognitive load will be significantly higher on individual contributors, and b) where does the job merging end? Does it even have an end?

...Then again, if the pay is that much better, who am I to disagree?!

This is still not great news for specialists and further confirms that the market wants T-shaped marketers. But if you don't mind also taking on adjacent tasks and a bigger job with fewer handoffs, you can potentially earn more than before as a freelancer!

Which IT services companies are getting more out of their people as AI changes how the work is done? 

Our research team looked at 37 listed IT services and outsourcing companies, from Accenture and EPAM Systems to Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys and Wipro. 

For each one, we compared how much revenue each employee brought in this year with two years ago.

Overall, the industry is still growing mostly by hiring. Over two years, revenue across the group grew 6.4% and the number of employees grew 4.2%, so revenue per employee rose just 2.1%. That matters because clients are already pushing for lower prices, and some are asking for discounts of up to 40% when contracts come up for renewal.

The results vary widely by company. Mid-sized firms such as Netcompany, Persistent Systems and Nagarro, along with Accenture and EPAM, are growing faster than most of the group and getting more from each employee. 

The large firms that do most of their work from India, including TCS, Infosys, HCLTech and Cognizant, are improving, but slowly. Wipro, Mphasis, Genpact and Hexaware Technologies now bring in less per employee than they did two years ago.

Imagine you're hiring a senior AI engineer in Dubai.

You've got a great salary on offer, an interesting project, a strong team and you're ready to start interviewing.

Theres just one small problem, the person you really want is currently working for a tech company in London.

They're earning good money. Their partner has a decent job. The kids are settled in school. They've just bought a house.

Now you're asking them to pack all that up and move 3,000+ miles away.

Suddenly, your brilliant job opportunity has got some fairly serious competition and thats before we even get onto the other companies trying to hire the same person.

Businesses spend a lot of time thinking about their competitors. Who's winning contracts, who's expanding, who's offering better products or services.

But when you're trying to recruit someone internationally, your biggest competition might be their mortgage, their partners career or the fact that their kids have finally settled into a school they love.

None of which you can solve by adding another few grand to the salary.

Ive had lots of these conversations over the years, and you quickly learn that the job itself is only part of the discussion.

What would make someone genuinely consider leaving a good position?
Would their partner be able to find work? 
What about schools, housing, the cost of relocating and whether the opportunity offers enough for the whole family?

Sometimes, after all those conversations, the answer is still no.

When you understand what someone actually needs to make a move, you've got a much better chance of putting together an offer they'll seriously consider.

Thats a big part of international recruitment. Knowing how to find the right people is one thing. Understanding what it would take to get them through the door is another.

If you're hiring internationally across AI, Tech or Digital Transformation, Im always happy to have a chat about the talent available and what it might take to attract them.

For a while the story about AI was simple and a little seductive. The models would solve everything, and you wouldn't need people in the middle.

It was never quite true, but it was loud, and loud sells.
 
What's become clear over 2026, especially the first half, is how much work sits between a frontier model and a result a business can actually use.
 
Here's the tell.

The frontier labs themselves are the ones admitting it, through their actions. They are building large deployment and services arms, hiring engineers, acquiring companies, pouring investment into the unglamorous job of making their models work inside real enterprises.

If the model alone were enough, none of that would be necessary. The people who build the models are quietly treating the model as the starting point, not the finish line.
 
You can see it in the market too, once you look past the early panic.

A few months ago the fear was that AI would simply wipe out services firms. Since then, some of the largest have had a serious run instead, because buyers rediscovered something obvious. Someone has to connect the model to their data, their decisions, their messy reality. The demand for engineers who can genuinely deploy this, by whatever name we give them this quarter, has only climbed.
 
The commercial shape of it will change, no doubt. The era of contracts for thousands of generic bodies is fading. What's rising is the premium on people who can make AI actually work in one specific business. Offer a company a hundred engineers who can do that well, and they'll take your call today.
 
None of this is a knock on the models.
It's a more honest picture of how value gets created with them.

The intelligence is extraordinary.
Turning it into outcomes is still real work, done by real people.

If you're deploying AI in your enterprise, where does the hard part actually sit for you, in the model, or in everything around it?

What happens when a consulting company gets paid for results instead of hours worked?
It sounds like a better deal for everyone. But I think there's a catch.
Reuters recently reported that major IT services companies are moving toward performance-based contracts as AI makes certain tasks faster and cheaper.
Some customers are asking for price reductions of 25% to 30%, while others want payments tied directly to productivity improvements and business outcomes.
On the surface, that seems reasonable.
If a technology provider promises to reduce operating costs by 20%, why shouldn't part of its compensation depend on actually delivering those savings?
But measuring results is rarely as simple as it sounds.
Imagine hiring a consulting firm to improve customer service.
The firm introduces AI tools, reduces response times, and cuts operating expenses. The numbers look fantastic.
But what if customers are now receiving less helpful answers? Or employees are spending more time correcting mistakes behind the scenes?
The project might meet its contractual targets while making the overall customer experience worse.
That's what concerns me about performance-based pricing.
The incentives only work when everyone agrees on what good performance actually means.
And choosing the wrong metric can encourage companies to optimize the numbers instead of solving the problem.
I'm not against outcome-based contracts. I actually think they could create healthier relationships between customers and service providers.
But they require trust, clear expectations, and a willingness to look beyond the easiest things to measure.
AI will probably make this debate more important across consulting, marketing, software development, and many other industries.
Because completing a task faster doesn't automatically mean completing it better.
If you were hiring an outside technology partner, would you prefer to pay a fixed project fee or link payment to measurable business results?

Abhishek Bartakke is building the alternative. Syncro1 is an outcome-based hiring platform where clients pay only when a placement succeeds, and it is the subject of our new outcome-based hiring interview on TechRecast.

Context: recruitment technology has spent a decade improving the top of the funnel — sourcing, screening, scheduling — while leaving the commercial model untouched. Syncro1's bet is that the model is the real problem.

The hard questions are technical and commercial:
• How do you define and verify a "successful, sustained placement" at scale?
• Where does the AI genuinely do work a rules-based matcher could not — and where is a human still better?
• Pay-on-placement shifts working-capital risk onto the platform. Does that economics hold across a full hiring cycle?

There is also a fair sceptic's question: contingency recruitment has existed for decades. Is outcome-based hiring a structural change, or a modern interface on an old model?

The bigger point: if vendors are paid for activity, no amount of software fixes the misalignment. You have to change who carries the risk.

One thing that stayed with me: Bartakke's argument comes from the inside — HR Business Partnering across high-volume, high-churn sectors where the gaps in traditional staffing are felt most acutely. That is a credible place to have found the problem.

The open question is whether practitioner insight becomes a defensible platform.

There is also a harder question for the platform itself: pay-on-placement is only as strong as the definition of success. If a placement is counted the moment a candidate joins, the model is easy to game. If it requires the hire to stay and perform, the platform carries real risk.

The question is not whether staffing needs better software. It is whether it needs a different contract. Syncro1 Pvt Ltd is a test of whether changing who carries the risk changes how the work gets done.

The UAE issued its federal data protection law in 2021. Five years later, according to published legal commentary, its Executive Regulations are still awaited.
That gap matters more than it seems. Federal Decree-Law No. 45 of 2021 already sets out the rights of individuals and the duties of organisations. Much of the operating detail is still missing, and every business handling personal data in the UAE is planning around it.
From a lawyer's perspective, three points deserve attention now:
1. The law reaches beyond UAE borders. It covers controllers and processors in the UAE, and also those abroad that process the data of people inside the country. DIFC and ADGM keep their own data protection regimes, so one corporate group can face several rulebooks at once.
2. It already speaks to AI. Article 18 gives individuals the right to object to automated decisions with legal or serious effects, including profiling, subject to exceptions such as prior consent. As hiring, credit and customer decisions become automated, this short article may turn out to be one of the most important in the law.
3. The clock has not started, but it will. Article 29 gives organisations six months to comply once the regulations are issued. That is a short time to map data, rewrite contracts and train staff. Waiting for the text is a risk in itself.
The institutional picture is moving too. The UAE created a federal authority for artificial intelligence and data in June 2026, which suggests that the two fields will increasingly be regulated together.
My research on digital privacy and cybercrime keeps returning to one lesson: a privacy right is only as strong as the rules and institutions that apply it.
If you run or advise a business in the UAE, what would you most like the regulations to clarify: cross-border transfers, breach notification or the role of the data protection officer?

Over half of enterprise data engineering capacity is spent keeping yesterday's pipelines alive.

That is Fivetran's 2026 Enterprise Data Infrastructure Benchmark, 500 senior data leaders at companies above 5,000 employees. 53% of engineering capacity goes to pipeline maintenance. The average organisation runs more than 300 pipelines, sees 4.7 failures a month, and burns around 13 hours resolving each one. 97% said those failures slow analytics or AI work down.

Fair warning on the source. Fivetran sells managed pipelines, so the ROI claims in that report deserve the scepticism you would give any vendor benchmark. The time split is the part worth sitting with, because it matches what engineering leads say out loud in almost every review I have sat in.

Here is the uncomfortable reading of it. If half the team is on upkeep, hiring does not fix the problem. You are not short of people. You are short of pipelines that tell you when they break.

Most of what gets called a data quality problem is a missing test. Most of what gets called a governance problem is a missing owner. Neither one is solved by a policy document, and both get quietly worse every time a new source gets bolted on under deadline.

So we build the boring parts first. Contracts on the inputs. Tests that run on write, not on complaint. Lineage you can follow from a number on a dashboard back to the row that produced it. One named owner per dataset, a person, not a team inbox. Slower in week one, and the only version still standing in month nine.

How many of your pipelines would tell you they had failed, before a stakeholder did?

Find the signal. Create clarity. Improve decisions.

We’re hiring an AI / Machine Learning Developer who wants to help strengthen disaster preparedness in the Pacific.

At Kahuto Pacific, we’re building tools to support Fiji’s National Disaster Management Office (NDMO)—bringing AI, geospatial data and local knowledge together to help identify flood risks, understand which communities are most exposed and strengthen preparedness before disaster strikes.

You’ll help turn aerial imagery, terrain data and machine learning into practical tools for disaster management teams. You’ll work alongside our survey and GIS specialists, with opportunities to learn from the people who understand these places and the challenges they face.

We’re looking for someone with strong Python and applied AI / ML skills, an interest in computer vision and geospatial data, and a willingness to collaborate and share knowledge.

As a Pacific-led company, we want to build technology and capability that stay in our region. If that’s something you want to contribute to, we’d like to hear from you.
